# Thrombocytopenia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Platelet and coagulation disorders > Thrombocytopenia*

[Original Article Link](/library/wT0hG2)

---

## Summary

Thrombocytopenia is a <u>platelet count</u> below the normal range (< 150,000/mmÂ³) that is most commonly due to either impaired <u>platelet production</u> in the <u>bone marrow</u> or <u>increased platelet turnover</u> in the periphery. Common causes of impaired <u>platelet production</u> include <u>bone marrow</u> failure, infection, <u>malignancy</u>, and <u>chemotherapy</u>/radiation. Additional etiologies include hereditary syndromes, such as <u>Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome</u> and <u>Alport syndrome</u>. In contrast, increased peripheral <u>platelet</u> turnover may be caused by autoimmune conditions, (e.g., <u>immune thrombocytopenia</u>), drugs (e.g., <u>heparin</u>), and other conditions (e.g., <u>TTP</u>/<u>HUS</u>, <u>DIC</u>/<u>sepsis</u>). Thrombocytopenia is often asymptomatic and found incidentally on routine bloodwork. Patients may notice <u>petechiae</u> or <u>mucosal</u> bleeding (e.g., bleeding <u>gums</u>, <u>epistaxis</u>) at lower <u>platelet counts</u>. Other patients with thrombocytopenia are clinically ill and have multisystem findings (e.g., acute infection, <u>liver</u> disease, <u>TTP</u>/<u>HUS</u>, <u>DIC</u>). Diagnosis should be confirmed with repeat testing (to rule out <u>pseudothrombocytopenia</u>) and underlying causes should be investigated and treated. Patients with active bleeding or neurological symptoms require emergency <u>platelet transfusion</u>, and in cases of immune-mediated etiologies, IVIG. Observation may be sufficient for patients who have stable medium-low <u>platelet</u> levels and no serious underlying condition. Patients with suspected <u>ITP</u> and low <u>platelet counts</u> (e.g., < 30,000/mmÂ³) are typically treated with <u>corticosteroids</u>, IVIG, or <u>splenectomy</u>.




See also “<u>Immune thrombocytopenia</u>”.

---

## Etiology

### Impaired <u>platelet production</u> in <u>bone marrow</u> [[1]](/library/hL0cxg)




<u>Bone marrow</u> conditions → ↓ <u>megakaryocytes</u> → ↓ <u>thrombopoiesis</u>




* <u>Bone marrow</u> failure: <u>aplastic anemia</u>, <u>paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria</u>

* <u>Bone marrow suppression</u>: drugs (e.g., <u>linezolid</u>, <u>daptomycin</u>, <u>valproic acid</u>, <u>valacyclovir</u>), <u>chemotherapy</u>, radiation

* Congenital thrombocytopenias: <u>Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome</u>, <u>Alport syndrome</u>, <u>Bernard-Soulier syndrome</u>, <u>Fanconi anemia</u>, <u>von Willebrand disease</u>

* Other congenital conditions: <u>Gaucher disease</u>

* Infection: <u>CMV</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>hepatitis C</u> <u>virus</u>, <u>HIV</u>, <u>mumps</u> and <u>rubella</u>, <u>parvovirus B19</u>, <u>rickettsia</u>, <u>VZV</u>, <u>dengue</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>: <u>leukemia</u>, <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>bone marrow</u> infiltration, <u>myelodysplastic syndrome</u>

* Nutritional deficiency: <u>vitamin B12 deficiency</u> and/or <u>folate deficiency</u> (e.g., in chronic <u>alcohol abuse</u>)

* Other: <u>necrotizing enterocolitis</u>





> [!NOTE]
> If <u>platelet production</u> is impaired, the number of <u>megakaryocytes</u> on <u>bone marrow biopsy</u> will also be decreased.




### Increased platelet turnover in the periphery




* <u>Immune thrombocytopenia</u>;  (<u>ITP</u>) and other autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u>, <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>)

* <u>Disseminated intravascular coagulation</u> (<u>DIC</u>) and <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura</u>;  (<u>TTP</u>) and <u>hemolytic uremic syndrome</u> (<u>HUS</u>)

* Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia (DITP): <u>Platelet</u>-activating <u>antibodies</u> cause a <u>hypercoagulable state</u> and simultaneous reduction in <u>platelet count</u>.

* The following drugs are most likely to be associated with DITP: [[2]](/library/INXYcA)[[3]](/library/rNXfcA)

* <u>Sodium-channel blockers</u>: <u>quinine</u>, <u>class I antiarrhythmics</u> (e.g., <u>quinidine</u>); , <u>valproate</u>, <u>carbamazepine</u>

* <u>Calcium-channel blockers</u>: <u>amlodipine</u>

* <u>Antibiotics</u>: <u>linezolid</u>, <u>vancomycin</u>, <u>TMP-SMX</u>, <u>penicillin</u>, <u>ceftriaxone</u>, <u>rifampin</u>

* <u>Antiviral agents</u>: <u>ganciclovir</u>, <u>protease inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>indinavir</u>); , <u>zidovudine</u>

* <u>Antithrombotic agents</u>: <u>glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>abciximab</u>), <u>heparin</u>

* Others: <u>oxaliplatin</u>, <u>suramin</u>, <u>ibuprofen</u>, <u>mirtazapine</u>

* See also <u>Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia</u> (<u>HIT</u>)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>: <u>preeclampsia</u>;  and <u>HELLP syndrome</u>

* Infection (see above)

* Post-<u>transfusion</u> thrombocytopenia

* Mechanical damage due to artificial cardiac valves or extracorporeal circulation (e.g., dialysis)





> [!NOTE]
> Increased peripheral turnover also increases numbers of <u>megakaryocytes</u> on <u>bone marrow biopsy</u>!




### Redistribution, dilution, and other causes




* <u>Liver</u> disease and chronic <u>alcohol abuse</u> (decreased production of <u>thrombopoietin</u> in the <u>liver</u>)

* <u>Splenomegaly</u>

* <u>Gestational thrombocytopenia</u>

* Thrombocytopenia following <u>transfusion</u> or <u>fluid resuscitation</u>

* <u>Pulmonary embolism</u> or <u>pulmonary hypertension</u> [[1]](/library/hL0cxg)

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/hL0cxg)




* Confirm the diagnosis in all patients:

* Repeat <u>CBC</u> and compare with previous <u>platelet counts</u>.

* Consider <u>peripheral blood smear</u> to exclude <u>pseudothrombocytopenia</u>.

* Investigate for underlying causes with a thorough history and routine <u>laboratory studies</u>.

* If the etiology remains unclear:

* Evaluate recent medication (see “Etiology”).

* Order additional investigations based on clinical suspicion, e.g., evaluation for <u>MDS</u> or other malignancies in patients > 60 years old with new-onset thrombocytopenia.

* See “<u>ITP</u>” if isolated thrombocytopenia with no other underlying cause detected.

* Evaluate for complications:

* Identify the source of hemorrhage in bleeding patients (e.g., see “<u>GI bleeding</u>”).

* Obtain <u>neuroimaging</u> for patients with <u>altered mental status</u>.

* See also “<u>DIC</u>”.





> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay treatment for diagnostic testing in patients with significant bleeding or new neurological symptoms.




### Routine <u>laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/hL0cxg)




* <u>CBC</u>: ↓ <u>platelet count</u> (< 150,000/mmÂ³); depending on the etiology, <u>anemia</u> or <u>pancytopenia</u> may be present.

* <u>Coagulation studies</u>: ↑ <u>bleeding time</u>

* <u>Peripheral blood smear</u>

* Abnormal <u>platelet</u> morphologies and cells

* <u>Platelet clumping</u> may be seen in <u>pseudothrombocytopenia</u>.

* <u>Renal function tests</u>

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>





> [!WARNING]
> A rapidly falling <u>platelet count</u> is worrisome, even if it is within the normal range (e.g., in <u>HIT</u>).




![Pseudothrombocytopenia](media/kezgsylmy19rpwood233g4x1.jpg)

Pseudothrombocytopenia

Consider additional <u>laboratory studies</u> or imaging depending on clinical features and results of routine <u>laboratory studies</u>

| Autoimmune disease | <br><br>* History of autoimmune disease<br><br>* Features of systemic autoimmune diseases, e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>rash</u>, <u>arthralgia</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Positive <u>autoantibodies</u> (e.g., <u>ANA</u>, <u>antiphospholipid antibodies</u>)<br><br> |
| <u>Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia</u> | <br>* Recent <u>heparin</u> use<br><br> | <br><br>* Positive PF4 <u>antibodies</u><br><br>* See “<u>HIT</u>” for further information.<br><br><br> |
| <u>HELLP syndrome</u> | <br>* <u>Pregnancy</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Abnormal <u>liver chemistries</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>LDH</u><br><br>* ↑ Urine protein<br><br>* See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Hypertensive pregnancy disorders</u>.”<br><br><br> |

| <br><u>Liver</u> disease and/or <u>hypersplenism</u>  <br> | <br><br>* <u>Stigmata of chronic liver disease</u><br><br>* Abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* Palpable organomegaly (i.e., <u>hepatomegaly</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>)<br><br>* Post-<u>liver transplant</u> [[11]](/library/4mX3fA)<br><br>* See “Etiology” in “<u>Cirrhosis</u>”<br><br>* See also “Pathophysiology” in “<u>Splenomegaly</u>”.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Abnormal <u>liver chemistries</u><br><br>* ↓ <u>TPO</u> levels<br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> abnormalities: e.g., <u>liver fibrosis</u>, <u>cirrhosis</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u><br><br><br> |

## Subtypes and variants

### Gestational thrombocytopenia [[12]](/library/n6Y7lJ)[[13]](/library/WGbPyE)




* Description

* A benign condition characterized by mild thrombocytopenia

* Most common during the second half of <u>pregnancy</u>

* Pathophysiology: likely due to increased circulatory volume during <u>pregnancy</u> (i.e., dilutional thrombocytopenia) and consumption and pooling of <u>platelets</u> in the <u>placenta</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>CBC</u>: ↓ <u>platelet count</u> (100,000–150,000 /mm³)

* Diagnosis of exclusion; additional evaluation is not necessary.

* Further workup to assess for more serious causes (e.g., <u>immune thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>HELLP</u>) is indicated in symptomatic patients or those with more severe thrombocytopenia (< 100,000/mmÂ³).

* Management: does not require treatment or change in <u>prenatal care</u> and delivery

---

## Differential diagnoses

See “<u>Differential diagnosis of platelet disorders</u>” for a comparison of findings in various etiologies of thrombocytopenia.




* Pseudothrombocytopenia: A spuriously low <u>platelet count</u> due to <u>platelet clumping</u> in vitro  [[1]](/library/hL0cxg)[[14]](/library/cmXaeA)[[15]](/library/1mX2eA)
* <u>Platelet clumping</u> can occur secondary to: [[16]](/library/7NX4cA)

* Pre-analysis collection factors : e.g., sampling technique , choice of <u>anticoagulant</u> used in collection tubes , delays in analysis, improper storage

* Disease factors : e.g., presence of <u>antibodies</u> to <u>EDTA</u> <u>anticoagulant</u>, autoimmune and inflammatory conditions (e.g., <u>cold agglutinin disease</u>), <u>neoplastic</u> disease (e.g., <u>multiple myeloma</u>), viral infections, drugs (e.g., <u>chemotherapeutic agents</u>)

* Dilutional thrombocytopenia: Falsely low <u>platelet</u> concentration due to <u>volume overload</u>; typically affects all other cell counts (i.e., associated <u>dilutional anemia</u> and <u>leukopenia</u>)





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

Patients with thrombocytopenia may be asymptomatic or acutely unwell if the thrombocytopenia is a feature of a wider syndrome such as <u>DIC</u> or <u>TTP</u>. Management depends on symptoms, initial <u>platelet count</u>, and the underlying condition.




### Approach [[1]](/library/hL0cxg)[[17]](/library/3dXSpC)




* All patients

* Treat any significant bleeding (see “<u>Emergency management of thrombocytopenia</u>”).

* Treat underlying cause (See “Etiology”).

* Immediately treat serious or life-threatening underlying illnesses (See “Treatment” in “<u>TTP</u>”, “<u>HIT</u>”, “<u>HUS</u>”, and “<u>DIC</u>”).

* Benign or mild illnesses may resolve spontaneously.

* Consider empiric treatment for <u>ITP</u> (e.g., <u>corticosteroids</u>, IVIG) if <u>platelet count</u> < 30,000/mmÂ³ without another apparent cause (see “Treatment” in “<u>ITP</u>”).

* Consider stopping medications that impair <u>platelet</u> function and increase bleeding risk, e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>.  [[17]](/library/3dXSpC)

* Mildly symptomatic or asymptomatic patients with a <u>platelet count</u> < 50,000/mmÂ³: Consult <u>hematology</u>.

* Asymptomatic patients with a <u>platelet count</u> > 50,000/mmÂ³: Repeat <u>CBC</u> in 1–4 weeks or if the patient becomes symptomatic.  [[1]](/library/hL0cxg)

* Decreasing or unchanging <u>platelet count</u>: Consult <u>hematology</u>.

* Increasing <u>platelet count</u>: Follow-up until <u>platelet count</u> has normalized.





### Emergency management of thrombocytopenia [[17]](/library/3dXSpC)[[18]](/library/KcXUWC)




* Indications

* Neurological symptoms

* Anticipated urgent <u>surgery</u> or invasive procedures

* Significant bleeding

* See also: “<u>Indications for platelet transfusion</u>.”

* Treatment

* If there is bleeding: Attempt <u>hemostatic control</u>.

* Urgently replace <u>platelets</u>.

* Immediate <u>platelet transfusion</u> (e.g., 1 unit of <u>platelets</u> IV; repeat as needed)

* If an immune cause is suspected: Administer IVIG (prior to <u>transfusion</u>). DOSAGE
